title: How to get generational wealth out of the AI bubble
description: Four rules: own only what survives a ten-year blackout, sell on a schedule and pay the tax, never borrow, buy what the bubble throws away.
body: Four companies will spend about $725 billion on data centers this year, up 77 percent on 2025, and for the first time most of it is not coming out of cash flow. AI-linked companies have issued roughly $140 billion of investment-grade bonds so far in 2026, about half of all investment-grade issuance in America. Alphabet sold a hundred-year bond in February to pay for chips it will depreciate in five or six. Meta's debt went from $36 billion to $84 billion in two and a half years. More than 80 percent of the S&P 500's gain this year came from AI names; strip them out and the index is up about two percent.

I am not saying it ends tomorrow. I am saying it ends, because every capital cycle financed with other people's money has ended, and the question for someone my age is not how to call the top. It is how to come out the far side of the bubble owning more of the world than you went in with. Here are my four rules. They are not sophisticated. The sophisticated people are the ones who get hurt.

One. The ten-year test. Before I buy anything I ask whether the company would still be standing if the world shut down for ten years, or if something catastrophic hit the economy in year three. Not thriving. Standing. Coca-Cola (KO) passes: people drank the product through two world wars, a depression and a pandemic, and the company has paid a dividend every year since 1920. Restaurant Brands (QSR) passes: thirty thousand restaurants selling humans the cheapest hot calories in their town, a demand that intensifies in a crisis rather than vanishing. Meta (META) passes, which surprises people. It owns the social graph of more than three billion humans, the graph does not depreciate, and whatever superintelligence turns out to be, the company has the cash flow to stay in that race from behind if it has to.

Now run the same test on SK Hynix, or Broadcom, or Marvell. Fine companies. But ask ten people who own them what the company sells, to whom, and what happens to the price of that product when the buyer's capital budget is cut in half. Most cannot answer. They own a ticker that went up, which is the only fact they know about it. The test is not "is this a good business." The test is "do you understand what kills it, and can it be killed." High-bandwidth memory is a commodity with a cycle. A social graph is not.

Two. Do not get greedy, and understand what greed looks like from the inside. What the people around you are experiencing is a number getting larger, which is a different thing from getting richer, and the number stays theirs only until they convert it. Almost no one converts it. They call themselves long-term investors when the actual mechanism is fear of the capital gains tax, so they never sell, and then the market sells for them at a price they did not choose. Pay the tax. Long-term federal capital gains top out at 23.8 percent; the bubble's discount is not capped. Decide in advance what you will sell and when, in writing, and move the proceeds into a separate account you treat as sealed, so that future you cannot talk present you out of the exit. If you want real structure there are legal forms of it: gifting appreciated shares, a charitable remainder trust, a donor-advised fund. What does not exist is a trick that makes a realized gain untaxed. Anyone selling you that trick is selling you a reason never to sell, and never selling is how the paper wealth of 2000 and 2021 turned back into paper.

Three. No leverage. None. No margin, no options you do not fully understand, no loan against the portfolio to buy more portfolio. Cash in, shares out, the end. Every bubble has a mechanism by which a correct long-term view gets liquidated at the bottom, and the mechanism is always a margin call. India's retail traders lost about $10 billion in derivatives last year. Korean margin debt is above 34 trillion won against an index that has more than doubled since the start of last year, and the forced selling has already started. These are people whose thesis might even be right and whose balance sheet will not let them stay to find out. Only money you can lose without receiving a phone call is money you can hold through a crash.

Four. Buy what the bubble is making distressed, because the bubble is a sorting machine and it is sorting wrong. Capital is draining out of everything that is not AI and into everything that is, and the exits are mispriced. Gold is about a quarter below its January record. Uber (UBER) sits near a 52-week low because the market decided robotaxis will eat it, while it throws off close to $10 billion of free cash a year. Netflix (NFLX) is down about 44 percent in twelve months on an advertising guidance cut. Brookfield (BN) owns ports, pipelines, transmission lines and the kind of assets that produce cash for fifty years regardless of which model is state of the art. These are unsexy, cash-positive businesses, and unsexy cash-positive businesses are the whole root of wealth that outlives a cycle.

Then hold cash on top. Real cash, boring cash, earning whatever it earns. When the correction comes the companies that are real will still be real, and the labs that matter will still matter; if Anthropic or OpenAI ever list, the time to buy is after the first drawdown and not on the first day. What will not survive is the layer that financed growth with debt it cannot service when revenue misses: the data-center shells, the GPU lessors, the clouds with one customer. Over-financed companies die in every cycle, not because the product was bad, but because debt has a maturity date and hype does not.
The AI bubble will make a small number of people generationally wealthy. Almost none of them will be the ones who bought the most AI.

title: A cartel of one
description: Indonesia mines two of every three tonnes of nickel, tried to ration its own ore, and watched the rally round-trip in ten months.
body: On a stretch of coast in Central Sulawesi that was grassland in 2013 there is now a 2,000-hectare industrial park with about 85,000 workers, fifty-odd tenants, a two-gigawatt coal plant and $34.3 billion of mostly Chinese capital in the ground. The Morowali park is what a policy looks like when it works. In 2020 Indonesia banned the export of raw nickel ore: if you wanted the rock you had to build the furnace next to it, and the Chinese did. Indonesia mined just over 30 percent of the world's nickel that year. In 2025 it mined 2.6 million of the world's 3.9 million tonnes, two of every three.

Everyone else shrank to fit. Australian output fell 54 percent last year; BHP (BHP) mothballed Nickel West in October 2024 and has promised only a review by February 2027. Philippine output fell 24 percent. Glencore (GLEN) guides to 70,000 to 80,000 tonnes this year, ten days of Indonesia. The Indonesians did it with high-pressure acid leach plants built for under $1.5 billion apiece and ramped inside a year; the Western plants of the last cycle, Goro and Ambatovy, cost nearly $6 billion each and took five years or more.

Which brings me to the price, which everyone assumes is high. It is not. Nickel averaged $15,000 a tonne on the LME in 2025, down 11 percent on 2024. The monopolist flooded its own market. So in February Jakarta did what a cartel does and cut the 2026 ore quota to 260 to 270 million wet tonnes, about a third below what it had approved for 2025. The metal ran from $14,000 in December to $20,000 on May 6, the highest since 2024. Then Indonesia's imports of Philippine ore rose 66 percent, smelter utilisation fell from 84 to 76 percent, lines in Sulawesi dropped below half capacity, and by October the ministry was cutting its ore benchmark and readying supplementary quotas. The International Nickel Study Group flipped its 2026 call from a 32,000-tonne deficit to a 19,000-tonne surplus. Nickel closed at $15,605 on October 28, roughly its level a year ago, with 279,000 tonnes in LME sheds. The rally round-tripped in ten months.

Indonesia owns the ore and China owns the furnaces, and when they disagree the furnace wins, because ore left in the ground costs nothing and a smelter left cold still owes the bank. The quota was set at compile time and renegotiated at runtime. Jakarta cannot run OPEC on an industry whose members are its own largest investors, and the investors have noticed: Tsingshan is pitching a park in Madagascar, Lygend wants a stake in Tanzania's Kabanga, and foreign direct investment into Indonesia fell 6 percent in 2025. Last week the Chinese-owned plants were reportedly discussing halving their own intermediate output. The producers are doing the rationing the state could not.

The cost of the boom is paid where the quota does not reach. In June 2025 a Greenpeace video of stripped islands in Raja Ampat, an archipelago holding about three quarters of the world's known coral species at the heart of the Coral Triangle, drew fifteen million views, and the president revoked four of the five permits there within days. The fifth belonged to Gag Nikel, a subsidiary of the state miner. Its suspension was lifted in September.

The Western answer is Talon Metals' (TLO) Tamarack deposit in Minnesota: 8.6 million indicated tonnes at 1.73 percent, Rio Tinto as partner, a Tesla offtake, $20.6 million from the Pentagon and a state scoping decision still pending. The company's own plan is production this decade, if the permits come. America imports 41 percent of the nickel it uses and nearly all of the primary metal, led by Canada and Norway, and that will not change because a Jakarta ministry changed a number.
A cartel of one is a country arguing with itself, and the furnaces are winning.

title: A garden hose on the seabed
description: Six hundred cables carry nearly all intercontinental data, four companies own the new ones, and under twenty ships exist to mend them.
body: On Saturday, September 6, 2025, two cables on the floor of the Red Sea off Jeddah stopped carrying light. One was SEA-ME-WE-4, the other IMEWE, both trunk lines between the Indian subcontinent and Europe; a third, FALCON, went down with them. Within hours Microsoft was warning Azure customers about traffic routed through the Middle East, Cloudflare was measuring delays of up to 30 percent between India and Europe, and Pakistan and the Gulf were running slow. The International Cable Protection Committee's early read was a merchant ship dragging its anchor. No one has shown otherwise. Repairs were put at two to six weeks: the ships need permits from several governments and must cross a war zone to get there.

The physical object is smaller than people imagine. Across most of an ocean a submarine cable is about the width of a garden hose, and the fibres inside it are the width of a hair. There are 607 of them in service, by TeleGeography's count this September, with another 102 planned, something over 1.5 million kilometres in all. The ICPC logs 150 to 200 faults a year, and 70 to 80 percent are fishing gear and anchors in shallow water. Sabotage is rare. It does not need to be common. The Red Sea carries about a quarter of the data between Asia and Europe through roughly fifteen cables threaded past one strait, and one anchor, if that is what it was, took out three of them on a Saturday.

The arithmetic from there is uncomfortable. Satellites carry well under one percent of international traffic; the FCC's figure for the United States is 0.37 percent. Everything else, every cloud region and every model weight, is a wire on the seabed, and the wires increasingly belong to four companies. Google has stakes in more than 30 systems, Meta in about 20, and TeleGeography counts Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon as stakeholders in over two-thirds of the systems now planned. Before the 1990s cables were built by consortia of national carriers: AT&T, British Telecom, Telstra. Now the cloud lays its own. A National Bureau of Economic Research paper this year puts about 70 percent of global data across at least one American-owned cable, up from under 20 percent in the early nineties. People argue about whether the internet is centralised. On the seabed it always was.

The laying is more concentrated still. Three firms build nearly everything: Alcatel Submarine Networks, 80 percent of which the French state bought from Nokia in 2024 for about €100 million; SubCom, the only American turnkey supplier, which Cerberus bought for $325 million in 2018 and which reached a record $4.7 billion backlog by 2024; and NEC. China's HMN Tech has most of the rest. Then the part nobody budgets for. Roughly 60 ships on earth can lay or mend a cable. Fewer than 20 do only repair. Eight of the sixty are under eighteen years old, nineteen are over thirty, the oldest dates from 1978, and the study TeleGeography wrote for the SubOptic Association last year has two-thirds of the maintenance fleet at the end of its working life by 2040. Replacing it costs about $3 billion over fifteen years, what four cloud companies spend on data centres in a day and a half.

The owners of the cables are the people who least want you to think about them, because a cloud that is a wire is a cloud with a location. In May Iranian officials floated charging a fee on the cables under the Strait of Hormuz and putting their repair in Iranian hands; an IRGC official has reportedly put the cables on the target list. Those lines carry less than one percent of global bandwidth. One repair ship sits inside the Gulf.
Nearly everything that crosses an ocean does it inside a garden hose, guarded by sixty ships and an assumption.

title: A labour-supply request in work boots
description: The people telling teenagers to become electricians are the people who will hire them. A purchase order is not career advice.
body: In September 2025 the chief executive of Nvidia sat in a British television studio and told the country's teenagers what to do with their lives. "If you're an electrician, you're a plumber, a carpenter, we're going to need hundreds of thousands of them to build all of these factories." The skilled craft segment of every economy, he said, "is going to see a boom." He said it again on Fox Business this August: hundreds of thousands of jobs for "people who build things, that make things with their hands." BlackRock's chief executive told an energy conference in March 2025 that he had warned the White House "we're going to run out of electricians." Blackstone's president promised a "huge boom in blue-collar employment." In July, leaders from BlackRock, Carhartt, Ford and Google formed an Alliance for America's Skilled Trades.

Take the pitch seriously first, because the shortage is real. The Census Bureau put data-centre construction at an $85 billion annual rate in August, up 73 percent on the year, while factory construction has fallen 32 percent from its 2024 peak. Electrical work is 45 to 70 percent of a data centre's construction budget, and the electricians' union near Washington has doubled its membership since 2018 to 14,700 and still cannot fill calls. A qualified electrician there earns about $59.50 an hour, better than $120,000 a year with benefits. About 20,000 electricians retire each year. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects electricians to grow 9 percent in the decade to 2035 and plumbers 7 percent, against 3.5 percent for all jobs. None of that is the problem.

The problem is who is talking and what they are buying. Every voice in that chorus is a buyer of electrical labour or a financier of the buildings that need it. When a customer tells you to increase production, that is not career guidance. It is a purchase order, written in the language of virtue, real work and hands and things, because a purchase order written in the language of wages would have to name a price and a term. The term is the capex cycle. Four companies will spend about $725 billion on data centres this year. The cycle will end as capital cycles end, and the message to the eighteen-year-old carries no date.

Now the numbers the pitch leaves out. Nine percent growth for electricians is 75,900 jobs over ten years, about 7,600 a year across the country. In 2024 the electrical contractors' association counted 120,000 apprenticeship applications, up from 70,000 two years earlier, already more than the positions on offer. The pitch has worked. A large data centre employs up to 1,500 people at peak construction and about 50 once it is finished; one analysis of federal payroll data found as few as 23,000 permanent data-centre jobs nationwide in 2024. The farmers in the same speeches are the one group projected to shrink, down 3 percent; ironworkers grow 1 percent. And an electrical apprenticeship takes four to five years. In a driven system, a response that takes longer to arrive than the force takes to change is always answering the previous push. In 2008 nearly one in four union construction electricians was out of work. Nobody who gave a speech in 2005 was laid off in 2009.

The equipment side has no such exposure. Caterpillar (CAT) sells the generators behind every server hall, Deere (DE) sells the tractor to a farmer the projections say will not be replaced, and Otis (OTIS) will service the elevators whichever tenant is in the building. Machines are bought once, at the top of the cycle. Labour is rented while the cycle lasts and returned when it ends.
Become an electrician if the work suits you; it is a good trade. Just notice that the man on television is not your guidance counsellor. He is your customer, and he would like the price down.

title: A truck with no driver still needs a dispatcher
description: Driverless freight is late, real and about to be cheap. The profit pools with whoever owns the loads, and Uber trades as if it owned trucks.
body: On Wednesday Aurora (AUR) told its shareholders it has built twenty driverless trucks. In February the target was two hundred by year end; that is now the end of February, revenue guidance has gone from a $15 million midpoint to $9 million, the quarter brought in $3 million against a $234 million net loss, and a company valued near $10 billion fell 7 percent after hours. Kodiak (KDK), down 87 percent since listing last year, signed its first binding highway contract: seventy-five trucks for a Fresno carrier, from 2028. Tesla's Semi reached volume production in September, seven years late, and is not autonomous.

Aurora's trucks have run half a million commercial miles with nobody aboard, including the thousand miles from Fort Worth to Phoenix no human may legally drive without stopping. A thousand trucks are promised for the end of 2027; one carrier has signed for five hundred, non-binding. The $250 million Aurora expects to burn this quarter is binding.

The 1,300 percent growth to 2036 I kept hearing is not Goldman's; it is a research shop's $1.3 billion last year becoming $17.7 billion. Goldman's April forecast is more useful: a $560 billion global market by 2035, cost parity with a human driver in the United States in 2028, and a cost per mile falling from $8.56 today to $2.03, against a driver at $2.55 now and $2.84 then. A truck that runs 80 cents a mile cheaper than a person and never hits an hours-of-service limit does not need to be clever. It needs to be allowed.

The forecast leaves something out. Once the driver is software, the truck is a commodity Volvo and Paccar build on their own lines, and the software is a per-mile licence sold by two or three vendors with no pricing power. Aurora and Kodiak both call themselves asset-light: the carrier buys the truck and rents the driver by the mile. Then who makes the money? Whoever has the loads. Matching freight to trucks across a continent is a demand problem, and one company has spent sixteen years on nothing else.

I own Uber (UBER), and the market has decided it is a ride-hailing company about to be eaten by robotaxis. It closed at $65.78 on Tuesday, a 52-week low, 35 percent below its high, fourteen times trailing earnings, with $10 billion of trailing free cash flow for the first time. Bookings grew 24 percent last quarter. Waymo left Uber's app in Phoenix in July and opens its own in Austin and Atlanta in 2028; it runs about 4,000 cars. Uber did 3.9 billion trips in a quarter, under half a percent of them autonomous. The disruption is real and small, and priced as large and certain.

Freight is the part nobody models. Uber Freight manages more than $20 billion of it; Aurora, Volvo's autonomous unit and Waabi have all hauled its loads between Dallas and Houston; Uber owns a piece of Aurora from selling it its self-driving unit in 2020 and backed Waabi's round. It builds no truck and writes no driver. In Rust I would call it a trait: the caller never learns which concrete type sits behind it, only that the method is implemented. The market is pricing the trait as one of the implementations.

The counter-argument is serious. A demand layer has power only while supply is fragmented. If Waymo ends up with most robotaxis and two firms with most trucks, they sell direct and Uber's take rate becomes a toll the owners refuse to pay. The founder of Uber Freight left last year to run operations at Waabi, which tells you where he thinks the power sits.

My bet is the other way, because every autonomy company is becoming a thin-margin seller of software by the mile, and none of them has a customer. A truck with no driver still needs someone to tell it where to go.

title: Boiling off in Qatar
description: A third of the world's helium sits behind Hormuz. Spot has tripled, fabs are rationed, and a Gulf peace is an AI trade nobody prices.
body: In March about two hundred cryogenic containers of liquid helium were stranded at Ras Laffan in Qatar, each holding roughly a million dollars of gas four degrees above absolute zero, each losing its load to boil-off within five or six weeks whether or not a ship came. The ships did not come. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed or contested since the United States and Israel struck Iran on February 28, and it carries about a fifth of the world's LNG and about a third of its helium.

The helium is the part nobody planned for. Qatar's North Field gas is 0.04 percent helium, nearly every atom an alpha particle shed by uranium or thorium in the rock below, and QatarEnergy strips it out as a by-product of liquefaction, a little over two billion cubic feet a year, sold to Air Liquide, Linde and Iwatani. Iranian drones shut Ras Laffan on March 2. Missiles on March 18 and 19 wrecked two LNG trains, 17 percent of Qatar's liquefaction and 14 percent of its helium, which the chief executive says will take about three years to rebuild. By August the helium plants were at a quarter of capacity. Force majeure on Qatari cargoes has just been extended to the end of December, the strait is moving perhaps 60 percent of normal crude under a US blockade of Iranian ports, and mediators were in Tehran this week.

So the price did what prices do when a third of supply vanishes and no substitute exists. Spot helium had doubled by the third week of March, with Europe near $450 per thousand cubic feet; by October a former Air Liquide executive put the spot move at a tripling, and long-term contracts, about 98 percent of the market and slow to reprice, are reported up 40 to 60 percent. American exports are up 70 percent since the war began, most of it to chipmakers in Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, because Exxon's LaBarge field in Wyoming is about a fifth of world supply and the United States, at 43 percent, is the only producer that can flex; Russia, the third, put helium under export permits in April. South Korea bought 65 percent of its helium from Qatar last year, and by June some Korean and Taiwanese fabs were getting half their normal volume. On October 23 the Department of Energy added helium to its critical materials list and named semiconductors first.

Why helium and not something else. It is the only substance still liquid at 4.2 kelvin, and the niobium-titanium magnets in an MRI scanner or a fusion experiment superconduct only below about ten, so a 1.5-tesla scanner sits in 1,500 litres of it and the periodic table offers no other coolant. In a fab the atom's lightness is the point: blown across the back of a wafer in the etch chamber, it carries heat to the chuck faster than any heavier gas, and it finds leaks in vacuum systems because nothing smaller exists to slip through them. Semiconductors take a fifth of the world's helium, roughly half the tools in a fab touch it, and a wafer not etched today is a GPU not shipped next quarter.

Here is what I think the market has wrong. It prices this war in Brent, above $117 last week, and in Qatar's LNG, which is why European gas is above €95. It does not price the inputs too small to carry a futures contract and too essential to do without, and helium is one of several. I own Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, and their capital plans assume the wafers get etched. A reopened strait is the cheapest upgrade to those plans on offer, and no analyst model carries the line.
Released helium never comes back; it is too light for the planet to keep. Qatar's has been leaving, a container at a time, since March.

title: Bug me last
description: Memory, then an API, then search, then the browser, then me. Every rung costs more than the one below it, and I am the most expensive.
body: Every time an agent asks me a question it could have answered itself, it tells me something about how it was built. The question is rarely hard. Which directory is the config in. JSON or YAML. Should I proceed. What it reveals is a lookup order, and the lookup order is wrong.

Here is the order I want. Memory first: what has already been established in this project, this session, this repo. Then APIs: the structured, typed, authenticated endpoints that return an exact answer in milliseconds. Then search: the open web, unstructured and noisy but wide. Then the browser: slow, visual, a last resort for pages that refuse to be anything but pages. Then, and only then, me.

The order is a cost gradient. Memory costs nothing. An API call costs a round trip and returns a fact with a schema attached. A search costs a round trip and returns ten guesses. A browser session costs seconds per click and returns pixels. A human costs minutes of latency at best, hours when I am asleep, and returns an answer that is itself a guess, because I usually know less about the current state of the task than the agent does. I am the most expensive oracle in the stack and the least reliable one. Treat me accordingly.

The industry has this backwards because of a confusion about what politeness is. Products that interrupt constantly are described as keeping the human in the loop, which sounds like respect and functions as delegation of blame. If the agent asks before every step, nothing it does is its fault. That is not safety. That is a design that has outsourced its judgment to the person least able to exercise it, at the moment they are least able to exercise it, and called the result alignment.

The honest version of the loop is narrower. Ask me when the action cannot be undone and the choice is a real fork: delete this, send that, spend money, publish. Ask me when the task as stated contradicts itself and no amount of reading will resolve the contradiction. Otherwise climb the ladder. Check what you already know. Hit the endpoint. Search. Open the page if you must. Take the most reasonable reading, write it at the top of your work so I can see which reading you took, and keep going.

I have been building a command framework in Rust where this principle is enforced by the compiler rather than by a prompt. The system definition is generated from the plugin's own types at build time, so a bound that will not typecheck is a compile error and not a surprise at registration. The point of that design is the point of the ladder: push every question as far upstream as it can go. Resolve it in memory if memory has it. Resolve it in the type system if the type system can. Resolve it in a schema. The human is where unresolvable things go, and the measure of a system is how few things it leaves unresolvable.

An agent that bugs me last has not stopped being careful. It has spent its carefulness on the rungs where carefulness is cheap, so that when it finally reaches me it is carrying a decision and not a question.

title: Every path ends in a wire
description: Three mines caved, flooded and collapsed in 2025, copper set records in 2026, and the energy transition turned out to be a metals trade.
body: On September 8, 2025, about 800,000 tonnes of wet mud moved through the Grasberg Block Cave in Papua and killed seven workers. Freeport-McMoRan (FCX) declared force majeure on the 24th, cut 2026 guidance for the world's second-largest copper mine by roughly 35 percent, and is still not at full rates. That was the third blow of the year. In May a seismic event flooded the Kakula mine in Congo and Ivanhoe (IVN) withdrew its guidance; its 2026 target is 380,000 to 420,000 tonnes from a complex meant to do 550,000. On July 31 a collapse at El Teniente in Chile killed six workers; Codelco suspended the mine's deep expansion this August over seismic risk, and an avalanche there killed two more on October 11. Escondida, the largest copper mine on earth, shut after a fatal accident on September 23.

Benchmark put the Grasberg loss alone at 591,000 tonnes through the end of 2026, 2.6 percent of a 23-million-tonne world. Global mine output fell 1 percent in the first seven months of this year and Chilean output fell 7 percent. Smelters short of concentrate are paying miners $272 a tonne to take it; in a normal year the money flows the other way. Copper began 2026 at $12,423 a tonne, printed $14,875 on September 10, settled a record $14,822 for cash on October 12, and sits near $14,500 this week, up a third on a year ago.

People say South America controls this market, which holds until you count. Chile mined 5.3 million tonnes in 2025 and Peru 2.7 million: 35 percent of the world together, and Congo, at 3.2 million, now out-produces Peru. What Chile has is a toll booth. Codelco, state-owned, digs about a quarter of the country's copper, booked 26,875 tonnes in 2025 that an internal audit found it had not produced, and mined 11 percent less in the first half of 2026. The royalty law in force since January 2024 pushes the effective tax burden on large miners to about 45 percent. Mining is 57 percent of Chile's exports. A country that dependent on one metal does not control the price. It prays to it.

Now the question I started with: what the shortage did to renewables. Less than you would think, and arithmetic says why. An electric car carries about 53 kilograms of copper to a petrol car's 22. At $14.50 a kilogram that is $770 of copper in the EV, and the whole rally of the past year added about $190 to it. Offshore wind uses about eight tonnes per megawatt against roughly one for a coal plant, so a megawatt of turbine carries $116,000 of copper, a rounding error on hardware costing millions per megawatt installed. The transition did not get expensive because copper did. Copper got expensive because the transition is real, because a data centre needs 20 to 40 tonnes per megawatt, and because China's grid spending rose 37 percent in the first quarter.

Which is what the climate deck and the mining deck both avoid saying. Solar, wind, gas, nuclear and the server hall disagree about everything except the conductor. Whatever makes the electron, copper carries it, with a resistivity only silver beats; aluminium, the one substitute, needs about 60 percent more cross-section to do the same job. The energy transition is a copper trade wearing a climate costume, and the costume is what gets the subsidy.

One caveat on the record. More than 700,000 tonnes sit in US warehouses, pulled in ahead of a Section 232 tariff decision on refined copper that has been pending since June and that Macquarie expects to pass New Year unanswered. COMEX stocks are up roughly 700 percent since February 2025 and forecasters still pencil in a small 2026 surplus. Some of the all-time high is metal hiding in American sheds.
Three accidents moved the price. The wire is what holds it there.

title: Every wire on earth, again
description: The money for the grid is finally arriving. The transformers are not. Electrification is now limited by a queue, not a budget.
body: Every power line on earth, strung end to end, runs to about 80 million kilometres. The IEA's count of what has to be added or replaced by 2040 to meet the targets governments have already signed is also 80 million kilometres. Not a share of it. The grid, again, in fourteen years, while the first one stays switched on.

The grid is the oldest machine most countries still run at full load. It has delivered power for over a century, and for most of this one it was treated as finished: global grid investment sat flat at roughly $300 billion a year while everyone argued about generation. The IEA's grids report said the figure had to pass $600 billion by 2030. Its 2026 investment report has network spending at about $550 billion this year, up nearly a fifth in twelve months. The money, for once, is arriving.

What is not arriving is the equipment. A large power transformer now takes up to four years to secure. A high-voltage cable takes two to three, a direct-current cable more than five, and transformer prices are up about 75 percent since 2019 while cable prices have roughly doubled. A new high-voltage line takes seven years or more; a data centre takes one to three. More than 2,500 gigawatts of generation, storage and large loads are stalled in connection queues worldwide, about 150 gigawatts of them data centres. In the whole of the last decade the world built about 1.5 million kilometres of new transmission.

Here is the physics of the mismatch, and I think it is the whole story. Any driven system has a relaxation time, and one forced faster than it can relax never settles into a new equilibrium; it lags the drive. A grid relaxes over five to fifteen years. The thing driving it, a hyperscaler's capital budget, changes by the quarter. The lag has a name on a utility's books. It is called the interconnection queue.

Now the demand the wire is supposed to carry. The world used about 28,200 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, three percent more than the year before, and the IEA expects 33,600 by 2030: roughly 1,100 terawatt-hours a year of new demand, against 700 a year over the previous decade. The United States uses about 4,200. So the world is adding a United States of demand every four years, and in the IEA's central scenario it adds more than two of them by 2035. Most people assume that is the AI. Globally it is not; data centres are less than a tenth of the growth, and the peak is set by air conditioning. America is different: data centres are about half of the 420-plus terawatt-hours it is set to add by 2030.

Which is where American Electric Power (AEP) comes in. Its summer peak was about 37 gigawatts last year. By May it had signed agreements for 63 gigawatts of new load by 2030, 41 of them in Texas, most of it data centres. They came to AEP because it owns about 2,100 miles of 765-kilovolt line, nine tenths of what exists in the country. Its five-year capital plan rose a third to $72 billion last October, to $78 billion in May and to $100 billion this week, with the rate base compounding at 13 percent or better through 2031. What the release calls "up to $21 billion of fixed cost offsets for residential customers" translates: under the old tariffs you paid for the hyperscaler's substation; under the new ones in Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia, the hyperscaler does. Last October AEP guided residential rates up 3.5 percent a year, and it earns a regulated return on every dollar of either. If I owned a utility, it would be the one that owns the wire everyone else is waiting for.
The power crosses the state in milliseconds. The wire it needs arrives in 2033.

title: Four hundred to one
description: India trades 394 rupees of derivatives per rupee of stock, nine in ten retail traders lose, and Jane Street made $4 billion there.
body: For every rupee of stock that changed hands on India's exchanges last fiscal year, about 394 rupees of derivatives changed hands on top of it. In 2016 the ratio was 14. The regulator, SEBI, publishes this number itself, in a study it released this August under the flat title "Profitability of Individual Traders in the Equity Derivatives Segment," which is the bureaucratic way of saying: we counted, and they lose.

They lose. Of the 8.75 million individuals who traded futures and options in the year to March 2026, 87.7 percent finished in the red. Together they lost 91,685 crore rupees, roughly $10 billion, and that was an improvement: the year before, 10.6 million people lost about $13 billion. Over five years the cumulative figure is 3.85 lakh crore, call it $45 billion, transferred from salaried Indians to whoever sat on the other side of the trade. About a third of these traders hold no stock at all. They are not hedging anything. They are buying weekly Nifty options on their phones the way their fathers bought lottery tickets, except a lottery pays out in the aggregate and this does not.

Who sat on the other side? For two years the single most profitable answer was a firm from New York that most of them had never heard of. SEBI's July 2025 order alleged that Jane Street made about 36,500 crore rupees, around $4.3 billion, from Indian index derivatives between January 2023 and March 2025, of which 4,843 crore was, in SEBI's view, the product of manipulating the Bank Nifty index: buy the constituent banks hard in the morning, let the index drag the options with it, hold a much larger short options position, then sell the banks into the close. SEBI barred the firm from the market. Jane Street deposited the $567 million in escrow within two weeks, had the bar lifted within three, and is still arguing the merits before the Securities Appellate Tribunal this month, where it has accused the regulator of moving the goalposts after the fact.

Hold the two facts together. The retail base loses on the order of $10 billion a year, and the best trading firm in the world found that market so rich that its 2024 India take, $2.3 billion, was more than a tenth of its global revenue. In 2025 Jane Street booked $39.6 billion in net trading revenue, more than JPMorgan's entire trading operation. India was part of the reason it could.

This is the part the moralists miss. SEBI's complaint was never that Jane Street was good. It was that one pattern, in one index, crossed from aggressive into manipulative, and that is a question for the tribunal. The structural fact is older and stranger. On top of a stock market worth roughly $5 trillion, India has built a derivatives market whose notional turnover runs at four hundred times the underlying, populated by tens of millions of individuals who are statistically certain to lose. There is no other market like it. The United States has a bigger options market in dollars and a far smaller one in participation. Korea had the wildest index options market on earth in 2011 and regulated it into a corner within a year. India's regulator is tightening too, with bigger lot sizes and fewer weekly expiries, and the number of active traders fell 18 percent last year. It remains the largest casino in the world where the house seats are open to anyone with a Mumbai office and a market-making license.

Which is why the right lesson for a hedge fund is not "stay away." Every quantitative firm I would want to own a piece of should have a desk in India and a compliance officer who has read the Jane Street order twice. The edge is not a trick. The edge is that a country of 1.4 billion people has decided, for now, to pay a toll of about $10 billion a year to whoever is fast enough to collect it, and has posted the tariff in a government PDF.
Toll roads are good businesses. The ones with a published rate are the best.

title: Four people and a gallon of diesel
description: The first coast-to-coast railroad in American history will be approved or killed by four board members on a clock that stops in August 2027.
body: A gallon of diesel moves a ton of freight nearly 500 miles on an American railroad. Union Pacific (UNP) burned 1.034 gallons per thousand gross ton-miles last quarter, and the number falls a percent or two a year because the physics is on its side: a steel wheel on a steel rail deforms by microns, a rubber tyre on asphalt by centimetres, and rolling resistance is the energy you lose putting the deformation back. Rail moves about 40 percent of long-distance ton-miles for 1.8 percent of transport emissions. Nothing on land comes close, and no single company has ever run the whole distance.

Union Pacific would like to be the first. On July 29, 2025 it agreed to buy Norfolk Southern for one share plus $88.82 in cash, $320 a share at the time and about $85 billion of enterprise value, promising $2.75 billion a year in savings and more than 50,000 route miles across 43 states, Pacific to Atlantic, under one dispatcher. Shareholders of both companies approved it in November with more than 99 percent of votes. If the regulator says no, Union Pacific pays Norfolk Southern $2.5 billion and walks.

The regulator is the Surface Transportation Board, and the decade in American freight is being settled inside a calendar almost nobody reads. The Board rejected the first application as incomplete in January: the railroads had projected no market shares past closing and left out the part of the merger agreement that defines when Union Pacific may walk. The revised filing arrived April 30. The Board accepted it on May 28 and froze the case for more detail on captive shippers, diversion and gateways. It lifted the freeze on August 18 and set the clock: comments November 18, replies February 16, briefs May 28, a decision by August 28, 2027. In September it refused to throw the case out early, as BNSF, CSX and five shipper groups asked, saying only that a deal of first impression deserved a full record.

First impression is the phrase that matters. This is the first merger judged under rules the Board wrote in 2001 and has never used, which require a Class I combination to enhance competition, not preserve it. The opponents say a coast-to-coast carrier cannot pass that test because its whole point is to remove the interchange, and the interchange is where a shipper gets a second quote. Union Pacific's answer is that the real competitor is the truck, and that autonomous trucks with no driver to pay or rest will take share from a network that loses a day or two at every hand-off. Its chief executive told a television interviewer this month he was 99.99 percent sure of approval and needs no divestitures. The chemical, fertilizer and grain shippers who would be left with one railroad in many places are less sure, and they pay the rate.

I think the shippers are right about the mechanism and the railroads are right about the truck, and the Board must pick which of two true things it fears more. What unsettles me is who picks. Five seats, four members: a chairman named by the President in January 2025, a vice chairman, a Democrat whose term runs to 2030, and a rail consultant sworn in this June. The fifth seat has been empty since the previous chairman was removed in August 2025 with no cause stated, a removal the Supreme Court's June ruling on independent agencies made all but unreviewable. No one has been nominated to it. There is no veto above these four, no appeal except to a court that defers to them, no ballot with their names on it.
The outcome will arrive as a press release with a number like 26-23. The railroad it describes will last a hundred years. The four people who decide it, you could not name.

title: Four signatures, one hand
description: UnitedHealth is the payer, the doctor, the pharmacist and the rail the money runs on. The fury is a signal. The structure is the problem.
body: Sixty-three cents of every dollar Optum Rx booked in 2025 came from another part of UnitedHealth Group (UNH). The pharmacy benefit manager filled 1.66 billion prescriptions and took in $155 billion; its largest customer is the insurer that owns it. Optum Health employs or affiliates more than 90,000 physicians, about one in ten in the country. Optum Insight owns Change Healthcare, the clearinghouse that moves 15 billion transactions a year and touches one in three patient records. Optum Bank holds the health savings accounts. One company is the payer, the doctor, the pharmacist and the rail the money runs on, and it booked $447.6 billion of revenue in 2025, up 12 percent.

CVS Health owns Aetna and Caremark. Cigna owns Express Scripts. Those three PBMs processed 80 percent of the country's prescription claims last year, and Humana runs the same model smaller. The industry's word for this is integration; the pitch is that one owner holding every step takes the friction out. A market, like a heat engine, runs on a difference: insurer and provider are the hot and cold reservoirs, and the price is the work done between them. Put both in one hand and there is no gradient and no work, only heat, and the heat is $155 billion of internal billing nobody outside the building ever negotiated.

The market noticed late. UnitedHealth closed at a record $596 a share in November 2024, worth about $560 billion. In April 2025 it cut its forecast and lost 22 percent in a day; what the release called "heightened care activity" was people using the insurance they had paid for. In May the chief executive left and the guidance went with him. By December the company was worth about $300 billion; it is back near $370 billion today. The 2025 medical care ratio was 89.1 percent: 89 cents of each premium dollar went to care.

In July 2025 the company disclosed criminal and civil Justice Department investigations into its Medicare billing, widened by August to Optum Rx and to how it pays its own doctors. A Senate Judiciary staff report in January found it captured more diagnosis codes than any other Medicare Advantage insurer and called risk adjustment "a major profit centered strategy." The company disputes it. On denials the record is also the Senate's: UnitedHealthcare's prior-authorization denial rate for post-acute care went from 10.9 percent in 2020 to 22.7 percent in 2022. Across the exchange market, insurers denied 19 percent of in-network claims in 2024; fewer than one percent were appealed.

On December 4, 2024, Brian Thompson, who ran the insurance arm, was shot dead on a Manhattan sidewalk on his way to the company's investor day. That was murder, and nothing in a denial letter or a 10-K excuses it. His killer pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges in August and will be sentenced in December; the state murder case is stalled on a double-jeopardy motion. What should trouble the company more than the trial is the public reaction, which was not grief. It told you how many people had met the structure at its worst with nobody to send the anger to, because the insurer, the doctor and the pharmacist were the same voicemail.

Violence does not break that structure. It hardens it: a company under threat gets sympathy, a bigger legal budget and a licence to call every critic dangerous. What breaks it is a statute. Arkansas tried in April 2025, banning PBMs from owning pharmacies; a federal judge enjoined the law and the appeal sits at the Eighth Circuit. Congress passed PBM transparency in February, effective in 2028. Transparency is what a legislature passes when it has decided not to touch ownership. The FTC settled its insulin case with all three PBMs by June; no settlement changes who owns whom.
The denial, the diagnosis, the prescription and the cheque carry four signatures from one hand.

title: Fourteen centuries of rock
description: Morocco holds 50 of the world's 73 billion tonnes of phosphate, nothing alive can substitute for it, and the seller has no shares.
body: A conveyor belt about a hundred kilometres long runs from the Bou Craa mine, in the part of Western Sahara that Morocco administers and the International Court of Justice has declined to call Moroccan, down to the Atlantic. It is the longest conveyor in the world, and the dust blowing off it is visible from orbit. Last year 2.02 million tonnes of rock went down that belt onto 36 ships for exactly three buyers, in India, Mexico and New Zealand. Everyone else has dropped away; the European Court of Justice ruled again in 2024 that the Saharawi have to consent, and they have not.

Bou Craa is about eight percent of what OCP digs. The number that matters sits in the Geological Survey's table: of the world's 73 billion tonnes of phosphate rock reserves, Morocco holds 50 billion, about 70 percent. China holds 3.4 billion, the United States one. Beneath the table, in the flat prose the Survey uses for every commodity: there are no substitutes for phosphorus in agriculture. There are none anywhere. The backbone of DNA alternates sugar and phosphate; the molecule every cell spends as energy is a triphosphate; bone is calcium phosphate. In my own corner of science, the way a cell tells a protein condensate to form or dissolve is to bolt a phosphate group onto the protein. Nitrogen you can pull from the air with enough natural gas. Phosphorus you dig.

Here is where the reserve number misleads. Reserves are about the future; production is about the price. China mined 110 million of the world's 250 million tonnes in 2025, Morocco 36, the United States 20. Divide the ground by the digging and China empties its reserve in about thirty years, America in fifty, Morocco in fourteen centuries. And this year's price shock had almost nothing to do with rock. A tonne of diammonium phosphate takes 1.5 to 2 tonnes of rock, 0.4 of sulfur and 0.2 of ammonia, and roughly 44 percent of seaborne sulfur loads in the Gulf. The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively shut for most of the eight months since the American and Israeli strikes of February 28; transits run in single digits a day against 85 before. Sulfur went from under $100 a ton in 2024 to above $1,000 by late summer. China, which exported 10 million tons of DAP and MAP in 2021, closed its exports in mid-March. Illinois DAP was $929 a ton on October 16, against $600 to $700 through 2024 and the first half of 2025. Morocco holds the rock. The sulfur comes from somewhere else, and this year somewhere else was on fire.

Washington noticed late. Since April 2021 the United States had charged a countervailing duty of more than 16 percent on Moroccan phosphate fertilizer, at the petition of Mosaic (MOS), which runs the Florida mines; Texas A&M puts the cost to farmers at $6.9 billion over five seasons. On June 29 the president declared an emergency and suspended the duty for eight months, and in August the first Moroccan cargo in five years, 54,000 tonnes of triple superphosphate, docked at New Orleans. The same summer Mosaic curtailed production in Florida and Louisiana for want of sulfur. The tariff protected a producer that cannot make the product without the Gulf, against a producer that owns the ground.

Which brings me to the strange part. OCP is 94 percent owned by the Moroccan state, the rest by a bank's funds, a pension fund and a university endowment; a 2008 law gives it the sole right to mine phosphate in the kingdom; it took in about $11.4 billion last year, up 17 percent. Its dollar bonds trade in Dublin. Its shares trade nowhere. You can lend to the most consequential monopoly in food. You cannot own it.
The last phosphate mine on earth will be Moroccan, and it will not have a ticker.

title: Not on the axis
description: Switch 2 sold 23.7 million units in thirteen months. The stock is down 42 percent, at thirty times a year Nintendo says will be worse.
body: On September 1 Nintendo raised the American price of the Switch 2 from $449.99 to $499.99, fifteen months after launch, with the console outselling the PlayStation 5 more than two to one. Companies do not usually do that in a console's second year. Nintendo (NTDOY) looked at memory prices driven up by the data-centre build, looked at tariffs, and decided the customer would pay. So far the customer has.

The numbers as of June 30: 23.68 million Switch 2 consoles sold since the June 2025 launch, 19.86 million of them in the first fiscal year against a launch-day forecast of 15 million. Sony's (SONY) PlayStation 5 shipped 1.6 million units in the June quarter. The Switch 2 shipped 3.82 million, and Nintendo described that quarter as down 34 percent, because the launch frenzy it was lapping was so large. The PS5 has 95.3 million consoles in the world after five and a half years. The Switch 2 is a quarter of the way there after one.

Then the software. Switch 2 owners have bought 58.17 million games, about two and a half a console. The original Switch, at 156.59 million units, ended up carrying ten games each over its life, 1.56 billion in total. Mario Kart World alone has sold 15.39 million copies. The Super Mario Galaxy Movie passed a billion dollars at the box office this spring, and Nintendo's income from licensing its characters more than doubled in the June quarter, to ¥34.8 billion. Sony owns a very good box. Nintendo owns a plumber that three generations recognise on sight.

The index committees file Nintendo under Communication Services, in a sub-industry called Interactive Home Entertainment, beside Netflix and Alphabet rather than beside the companies that make the television it plugs into. The classification is more honest than it looks. Nintendo is a media company that happens to manufacture its own distribution.

Here is how it wins, and it is the way it has won since the Game Boy. It refuses the spec war. Sony and Microsoft compete on one axis, rendering power, and on that axis Nintendo has been losing by choice since the Wii; the trick is that Nintendo is not on the axis. It sells a box good enough to run Mario, sells the box at a margin rather than as a loss leader, and then sells the software at a much fatter margin for seven or eight years to an installed base no other publisher can reach. Its customers are children. Children become parents, and parents buy the box they remember.

Now the price. The shares closed at ¥14,795 in August 2025 and trade near ¥8,500 today, down about 42 percent, for a market value around ¥9.8 trillion, roughly $63 billion. On trailing earnings that is 21 times. On forward earnings it is about 30, and the gap between those two numbers is the whole argument. Nintendo's own forecast for the year to March 2027 is 16.5 million consoles against 19.86 million, net sales down 11 percent to ¥2.05 trillion, profit down 27 percent to ¥310 billion, with about ¥100 billion of memory and tariff costs written into it. The market is paying thirty times a year the company itself says will be worse.

Is that right? Partly. Nintendo guides low; the 15 million became 19.86 million, and sell-through is running ahead of the original Switch at the same point in its life. But the memory squeeze is real, the price rise will cost units, and a $500 console is a different purchase from a $450 one in a household paying more for everything else. I would own it below ¥8,000, and not as a console cycle. I would own it as the only media company whose audience is replaced every seven years and arrives already knowing the characters.
Mario is forty-five years old. His customers are seven, and they always will be.

title: One percent of the light
description: Fifty thousand tin droplets a second, picometre mirrors, one company, sold out through 2028. The market still trades it like a cyclical.
body: Fifty thousand times a second a droplet of molten tin, 25 micrometres across, falls through a vacuum chamber and a carbon-dioxide laser hits it twice. The first pulse flattens it into a pancake. The second turns the pancake into a plasma at about 220,000 degrees Celsius, forty times the surface of the sun, and the tin ions, relaxing, give off light at 13.5 nanometres. That wavelength is the whole point and the whole problem. Nearly everything absorbs it, air and glass included, so no lens can focus it. Mirrors do the work, about ten of them, each a hundred alternating layers of molybdenum and silicon, each reflecting at most 68 percent. Ten reflections later, about one percent of the light that leaves the plasma reaches the wafer. Zeiss polishes those mirrors for two to three years apiece to a roughness measured in picometres, a fraction of an atom; scaled to the area of Germany, the tallest bump would stand under a millimetre.

One company on earth assembles this into a machine that works: ASML (ASML), in Veldhoven. A standard EUV scanner costs around $180 million. The High-NA version costs about $400 million and only about a dozen exist; Intel has run more than a million wafers through its machines, Samsung plans volume production on them in 2028 and TSMC in 2030. Last year ASML recognised revenue on 48 EUV systems and €32.7 billion of sales. On October 14 it reported a record quarter, €11.7 billion at a 57.5 percent gross margin, €4.1 billion of it EUV. In January it guided 2026 at €34 to €39 billion. It now says €44 to €45 billion, and €44 billion was the floor of the 2030 plan it laid out in November 2024: the bottom of its own decade target, four years early. Supply as planned for 2027 and 2028, the chief executive said, will not meet demand. Customers asking to reserve slots for 2029 and 2030 are being told to wait.

China has never been allowed an EUV machine. The Dutch do not license them, and since 2023 and 2024 the better deep-ultraviolet immersion tools have needed licences too, granted case by case. So Chinese fabs bought the older ones, more than $13 billion on roughly 180 NXT:1980i scanners in 2024 and 2025 by one count, and China was 41 percent of ASML's system sales in 2024, 33 percent last year and 23 percent in the quarter just reported. In Washington the MATCH Act, introduced in April, would end even that: all immersion lithography and the servicing of tools already installed, with the Netherlands given 150 days to copy the rule or watch the foreign direct product rule do it for them. It was folded into the Senate defence bill, and the Senate blocked that bill on July 14 in a fight over paying for the Iran war.

Now the price. The company whose supply is sold out for three years, whose nearest competitor does not exist, whose customers are begging for 2030, fell nearly two percent on October 14 and another two after hours because sales came in at €11.66 billion against a consensus of €11.72 billion. Half a percent. The shares have traded between $946 and $2,000 in twelve months, the range of a semiconductor-equipment cyclical, and ASML was one for decades, when fabs ordered scanners in waves and cancelled them in waves. The market still prices the quarter and not the queue. At 36 times next year's earnings it is not cheap, but its own January guidance was eight billion euros short, and the price increases on its critical tools only begin to show in 2027. If I were going to own one semiconductor company it would be the one that does not make semiconductors.
One percent of the light reaches the wafer. Every chip at the frontier is drawn with that one percent.

title: Qatar buys American
description: The world's second-largest LNG exporter just signed to buy 7 million tonnes a year of US gas. It is buying insurance on its own strait.
body: On October 22 QatarEnergy signed to buy 4 million tonnes a year of liquefied natural gas from Cheniere (LNG), half from Sabine Pass and half from Corpus Christi, at Henry Hub plus a fixed fee, through 2054. A week later it signed for 3 million more from Woodside's (WDS) plant in Louisiana, twenty years, first cargoes in 2030. The country that shipped 82 million tonnes of LNG in 2025, a fifth of everything traded on earth, is now, by its energy minister's own count, the largest buyer of American LNG, and he says the final number will be "much higher."

The reason is a date. On February 28 the United States and Israel began striking Iran, and Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carried a fifth of the world's LNG. In early March Iranian drones hit Ras Laffan; QatarEnergy halted production and declared force majeure. Then a missile strike disabled two of the fourteen trains there, 12.8 million tonnes a year, 17 percent of Qatar's capacity, repair time three to five years. A ceasefire in April, an agreement in June, a collapse in July, a US blockade of Iranian ports reimposed on July 14 and still in force. The force majeure now runs to year-end. The Dutch benchmark passed €97 a megawatt-hour this week, its highest since 2022, and Asian spot is above $31 per million British thermal units against $2.60 at Henry Hub.

Read the Cheniere contract against that spread and it is not a gas purchase at all. Qatar has 77 million tonnes of capacity and is building toward 142; it needs no Louisiana molecules. What it has bought is an option on the strait: twenty years of gas that loads on a coast nobody can close, priced off the Gulf Coast and resold at the price the Gulf sets. The minister said so almost plainly, that pipelines around Hormuz "can be also targets" and that these deals need no capital and earn money the day the strait shuts. The tenant of the most dangerous waterway on earth has bought insurance in Texas.

Here I part from the people pricing this as a golden decade for American gas. The supply wave was real before the war and is still coming: 234 million tonnes a year of liquefaction is under construction or approved worldwide, nearly half of it American, on top of 525 in operation. Venture Global (VG) closed $8.6 billion for the second phase of CP2 in March; Commonwealth and Delfin followed; the Energy Department has approved more than 18.6 billion cubic feet a day of exports since the January 2025 order ended the permitting pause, and first-half exports ran 23 percent above last year. Most of that gas is sold at Henry Hub plus a fee: the seller is paid for liquefaction and the buyer owns the spread.

So the question is what the spread looks like in 2030, when the plants being financed at today's $31 arrive. The IEA says the war delays the easing effect of the wave by at least two years and removes about 15 percent of the new supply expected through 2030. Delays, not cancels. Qatar's undamaged trains restart within a week of a peace deal, the first North Field expansion train is slated for early 2027, and the buyers shopping now did the opposite when the price spiked: Pakistan's first-half imports fell 47 percent, India burned coal, China took 12 percent less for four months. Demand at $31 is demand that has already started leaving. A liquefaction train is a thirty-year asset sanctioned in an eight-month price spike, and a fixed fee only looks fixed until the person paying it runs the arithmetic on a $9 Asian market in 2031.
The strait will reopen. Every contract signed this month is a bet on when, and the party best informed about the answer is the one that has started buying.

title: Rationing a metal the chemists are deleting
description: Congo shut its border, sent cobalt hydroxide up fourfold, and now watches the price fall: the cathode that needed the metal is retiring.
body: Every article about Congo's minerals contains the number $24 trillion, and I have yet to find one that shows the arithmetic, so I do not use it. Here are numbers somebody did count. In 2025 the Democratic Republic of Congo mined 230,000 of the world's 310,000 tonnes of cobalt, 73 percent, and holds 6 million of the 12 million tonnes of known reserves. Half the metal still in the ground sits in one country, and China refines about four fifths of what comes out.

On February 22, 2025, with cobalt below $10 a pound at a nine-year low, Kinshasa closed the border to it. Exports stopped for eight months. In October the ban became a quota: 96,600 tonnes a year for 2026 and 2027, 9,600 of them reserved for the state, from a country that had just mined 230,000. Exports were cut by more than half by decree, with no mine closing and no ore running out: the purest price-setting experiment any commodity has run this decade.

It worked, for a year. Cobalt averaged $21 a pound in America in 2025 against $16.77 in 2024; hydroxide out of Congo roughly quadrupled from where it stood before the ban; by late April 2026 metal was assessed near $56,000 a tonne. Then the rationer met the variable it does not control. By August the agency that sets the quotas was saying it might cut them further "to help restore market balance," which is what a cartel says when the price is falling. On October 28 cobalt was about $34,600 a tonne, down 29 percent in a year and 12 percent in a month.

The miners told you who they are by how they responded. CMOC (3993.HK), Chinese, runs Tenke Fungurume and Kisanfu and produced 117,549 tonnes last year, more than half of Congo's output and about 38 percent of the world's, from two mines. It kept its 2026 guidance at 100,000 to 120,000 tonnes against an estimated export quota near 31,000, so most of what it digs goes into a stockpile to wait. Glencore (GLEN) went the other way: its cobalt output fell 46 percent in the first half of 2026, Mutanda produced none, and the company says its Congolese assets now prioritise copper, with the cobalt held in solution to be sold "as export regulations evolve." Copper is at a record. Cobalt is the thing you leave in the tank. Canada, where it comes up as a byproduct of nickel, mined 3,500 tonnes in 2025, eleven days of CMOC. Indonesia mined 44,000, 14 percent of the world, as a byproduct of its nickel acid-leach plants, and no quota in Kinshasa reaches it.

Congo has rationed a metal the battery industry has spent a decade designing out. Cobalt's job in a cathode is structural: it keeps the layered nickel-manganese oxide lattice ordered while lithium moves in and out, and stops nickel wandering into lithium's sites. Lithium iron phosphate uses a phosphate framework rigid enough to need no cobalt at all, and it took 51 percent of the global battery market in 2024 and 79 percent of that year's growth. Cobalt-bearing chemistries fell from 60 to 53 percent of EV battery demand in one year. Within the chemistries that still use it, moving from an equal nickel-manganese-cobalt mix to the 8:1:1 formula cuts the cobalt per kilowatt-hour by more than half. An EV carries five to ten kilograms. The number is falling in both directions, by share and by dose.

OPEC rations a molecule nobody has replaced. Kinshasa is rationing one that already has a replacement with a lower bill of materials and a better safety record, and every month the price sits above the cost of switching, more cathode lines switch. The quota does not create demand. It brings forward the day the demand leaves.
The quota runs to the end of 2027, which is longer than the chemistry will wait.

title: Seventeen years for 400 points, eighteen months for 7,000
description: Seventeen years took the KOSPI from 2,000 to 2,400; eighteen months took it to 9,385. Margin did the last leg, and margin runs both ways.
body: On October 15, Korean brokerages sold 80.5 billion won of their customers' shares without asking them. A week earlier the daily figure had been 6.4 billion. Between the two, the KOSPI fell seven straight sessions, from about 6,900 to 5,500, and the margin loans underneath it, above 34 trillion won on October 13 for the first time since July, began shrinking the only way they shrink quickly: by being called.

The run-up needs dates. The KOSPI first closed above 2,000 in July 2007. It ended 2024 at 2,399, with a year above 3,000 in 2021. Seventeen years, four hundred points, and a literature on the Korea discount.

Then it closed above 4,000 last October, 5,000 in January, 6,000 in February, 7,000 in May, 8,000 three weeks later, 9,000 in June, and touched 9,385 on June 19. Seven thousand points in eighteen months. It then fell 44 percent in six weeks, to 5,263 on July 29, recovered to 7,100 by September, and gave up a fifth again in the first half of October. It closed Wednesday at 6,012 and Thursday at 5,938. That is not the chart of a stock market. It is the chart of a margin account.

The earnings are real, which is the dangerous part. SK Hynix reported this week: revenue of 104.6 trillion won, up 328 percent, an operating margin of 79.7 percent, memory sold out through 2029. Samsung made 107 trillion won of operating profit in the same quarter and promised 90 to 110 trillion won of dividends and buybacks. Two companies sit atop an index in a country where more than half of last quarter's growth surprise came from chips, private consumption fell at its fastest rate in four and a half years, and bank delinquencies are at a ten-year high. The index is the memory cycle. The country is not.

The retail investor's response was to borrow. Margin loans rose from 28.9 trillion won at the end of July to 34.3 trillion by October 12, up nearly a fifth, while cash in brokerage accounts fell 7 percent to 96.9 trillion. A market without leverage damps its own fluctuations, because a lower price finds a buyer. A market with 34 trillion won of margin amplifies them, because a lower price finds a margin clerk.

Forced sales rose 12.7-fold in a week, unsettled receivables reached 1.24 trillion won, and the margin balance dropped almost a trillion in a single day. It has since settled below 30 trillion, and on October 27 retail investors net sold 949 billion won while foreigners bought. The forced selling did what the dip could not: it broke the loop, for now.

The government has not been a bystander. On Thursday the president's senior secretary for policy apologized in the National Assembly for single-stock leveraged ETFs, products paying twice a stock's daily move, whose launch, he said, coincided with a period of repricing. Daily double leverage in a market that moves 6 percent on a Wednesday turns volatility into losses even when the stock ends where it began, and the state waved it through.

So, a reset. I will not name a date, only what has already happened: the index has been cut by 44 percent once and 20 percent once in four months, and the forced selling that did the second cut began with margin debt at 34 trillion won. The next leg begins wherever the margin balance sits when memory prices stop rising, and memory prices have never not stopped rising. Hynix says the shortage runs through 2030. The whole trade is a bet on that word, through.

The photograph above these stories is usually the same one: a wall of screens in the dealing room at Hana Bank's head office in Jung-gu, showing the KOSPI and the KOSDAQ. The screens show the index. They have never shown the loans.

title: Six times the demand, the same price
description: Lithium demand has grown six-fold since 2017 and the price is back where it started. The rock was never the scarce part.
body: In the middle of May a tonne of battery-grade lithium carbonate traded above 200,000 yuan on the Guangzhou futures exchange, a two-year high. On October 22 the main contract closed at 94,180. In dollars, Fastmarkets' seaborne assessment went from $24.50 to $25.80 a kilogram on May 11 to $12.80 to $15.00 on October 27. Nothing happened to the metal. Zimbabwe halted concentrate exports in February, a CATL mine in Jiangxi stayed shut, the market decided there was a shortage; then two Australian mines restarted, China's main price reporter restated national inventory upward by roughly 100,000 tonnes in a single September morning, and a bearish Goldman note on October 12 helped take the contract down 11.8 percent in a day.

If I were going to own lithium at all I would own the people who dig it rather than the futures, and the last five months show why neither has been comfortable. The chemistry is why I keep coming back, so let me get it right in two sentences. Lithium is element three, the lightest metal there is, and its standard reduction potential is about minus 3.04 volts, the most negative on the table, which is why it sits at the anode: a cell built on lithium delivers more voltage than one built on anything else. Energy is charge times voltage, and lithium supplies both terms, the most volts per cell and, because each atom weighs almost nothing, the most charge per gram. That is the whole bull case, and it is true.

Here is what the bull case leaves out. In 2017 the world consumed about 41,500 tonnes of lithium and battery-grade carbonate averaged $13,900 a tonne. In 2025 the world consumed about 263,000 tonnes, more than six times as much, and the American annual average was $9,000. Batteries went from 46 percent of demand to 88. Demand did what the decks promised, and the price, after a visit to $63,700 in 2022, came all the way back, because lithium is not scarce. It is dissolved in salt flats and locked in hard rock across Australia, Zimbabwe, Brazil, Mali and Argentina, and every one of them answered the 2022 price within three years. Scarcity is a story about rocks. Price is a story about how fast people dig, and people turned out to be quick.

The geography is the part I find beautiful. Under the salt crust of the Salar de Atacama in northern Chile the brine is pumped up into ponds, and the desert sun does the first stage of refining for free. That salar, Chile's corner of the lithium triangle it shares with Argentina and Bolivia, gave the world 56,000 tonnes last year, a fifth of mine supply and not the 30 percent people still quote; Australia's hard rock gave 92,000 and China 62,000. SQM (SQM), which pumps the Atacama alongside Albemarle (ALB), folded its operation last December into a joint venture with the state copper company that runs to 2060, which is Chile's way of saying it has noticed what the brine is worth.

The majors have voted with cash. Rio Tinto (RIO) paid $6.7 billion for Arcadium in March 2025, buying Argentine brine near the bottom of the cycle. Standard Lithium (SLI) and Equinor are a final investment decision away from pulling 22,500 tonnes a year of carbonate out of the Smackover brine under southwest Arkansas, with $225 million from the Department of Energy attached and first production pencilled for 2028. Until then the United States has one producing operation, Albemarle's ponds at Silver Peak, Nevada, so small that the Geological Survey withholds its output to protect the company. A country paying for a battery supply chain mines almost none of the lithium.

Lithium carbonate was a psychiatric drug before it was a battery; an Australian doctor began giving it to manic patients in 1949, and medicine is still one percent of demand. The salt has steadied minds for seventy-seven years. It has never once steadied a price.

title: Sixteen years on a five-year chip
description: Digital Realty just booked a record quarter. I still pass: six tenants, sixteen-year leases on five-year chips, and power it does not own.
body: After the close on October 29 Digital Realty (DLR) reported the best quarter a data-centre landlord has ever reported. Revenue of $1.9 billion, up 21 percent. New leases worth $855 million a year of rent, a record. A backlog of signed leases not yet paying, $2.5 billion, also a record. Guidance raised, dividend covered, a Moody's upgrade in hand. The stock rose less than two percent after hours, to about $186, which is 22 times this year's core funds from operations for a company whose tenants cannot sign fast enough.

Read the same release as a creditor and it looks different. Of the $627 million of new rent at Digital Realty's own share, $474 million, three quarters, came from hyperscale deals above a megawatt; the three largest were 60 megawatts or more each. Management offers as diversification that six different hyperscalers have been the top signer over the last seven quarters, which is another way of saying six customers drive the business. The weighted average lease it signed runs about sixteen years. It takes seventeen months from signature to the first rent cheque. The development pipeline, about 1.5 gigawatts under construction, is 63 percent pre-leased, so the other 37 percent is being built on faith, and the company will spend $4.25 to $4.75 billion on it this year, against $2.9 billion of shares sold into the market since January and about $19.5 billion of debt outstanding.

Nobody puts the mismatch on a slide. The landlord signs for sixteen years. The tenant depreciates the hardware inside the building over five or six, and the only reason to want a 60-megawatt hall in Indianapolis is that a capital budget in Seattle or Mountain View says so this year. Jefferies counted more than 80 percent of the S&P 500's gain this year, through May, as coming from AI names; without them the index was up about two percent. The tenants' appetite for halls is a function of that same enthusiasm. A REIT is being paid rent by the boom and has promised its own lenders the rent will keep arriving long after the chips in the racks are scrap.

In Rust the compiler refuses a reference that outlives the value it points at. A sixteen-year lease on a hall whose tenant's reason to occupy it is written off in five is exactly that reference. Real estate has no borrow checker; it has a credit cycle, and the check runs at the worst possible moment.

Then there is power, which the landlord does not own. Digital Realty's own call mentioned the long queues and constraints across Ohio and the nine-cent power in Indiana it moved toward instead. A data centre is a transformer with an office attached; the asset the tenant actually needs is the utility interconnection, which the REIT rents from a monopoly on terms it does not set. An analyst on the call put the build cost at roughly $15 million a megawatt. That is the price of a building whose value depends on a wire the builder does not control and a tenant whose budget it does not see.

I am not short. Shorting a landlord with a $2.5 billion backlog and investment-grade tenants is how people lose money arguing with a cycle. I own the tenants instead: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta. If the capex holds, they get the compute and I get the earnings. If it does not, they stop signing, and the stopping shows up first in the backlog of whoever built the shell. Equinix (EQIX) runs the other model, thousands of tenants renting cabinets and cross-connects rather than six renting halls, and it is the version of this business I would look at first if I looked at all. The newer single-tenant landlords are Digital Realty's trade with fewer customers.
The landlord has lent a building for sixteen years to a reason that lasts five.
