title: The $2.8 billion consolation prize
description: Netflix won the streaming war, was paid $2.8 billion to lose the bidding war, and sits at a 52-week low. I own a lot and I want an activist.
body: In February Paramount wired Netflix (NFLX) $2.8 billion for the privilege of buying Warner Bros. Discovery instead of it. Netflix had agreed in December to take the studio and HBO for $82.7 billion, then went all-cash at $27.75 a share in January; Paramount came over the top at $31, about $111 billion for all of Warner rather than just the studios, and Warner's board took it. Netflix declined to raise. The deal closed on October 6 and the combined company is called Skydance. Netflix walked away with the break fee, no $83 billion acquisition to digest, and a share price that has since fallen through the floor.

I own a large position. The stock closed at $62.05 on October 29, a 52-week low, down about 44 percent in a year from a high of $116.73. The quarter that did the damage, reported October 20, was a beat: revenue of $12.9 billion up 12 percent, operating margin 34.6 percent against 28.2 a year ago, earnings up 47 percent, $4.8 billion of buybacks, the most ever. It was punished for cutting its 2026 advertising forecast from about $3 billion to about $2.7 billion, and for a line in the letter admitting "some investor concern about our view hours growth."

Hold those two numbers next to each other. Three hundred million dollars of ads arriving a few quarters late, against a company that will do $51 billion of revenue this year at a 31.5 percent margin and generate $12 billion of free cash. The market took about $200 billion off the valuation for that.

The war is over and Netflix won it. The world holds 2.24 billion online video subscriptions and spent $176 billion on them last year, passing pay television for the first time. Netflix had more than 325 million of those paying households at the end of last year, by far the largest, and it is the only pure streamer earning a margin a packaged-goods company would envy. The rivals that remain are divisions of a phone maker, a retailer and a theme-park operator, plus Skydance, which lined up $54 billion of debt commitments to assemble a library. The American household holds about four paid video services and pays about $69 a month for them, and 73 percent say they are tired of the price rises. Churn across the industry runs near 40 percent a year. Netflix's churn after this year's increases was better than it forecast.

Which brings me to the thing I actually want, and the irony in wanting it. Pershing Square bought about 3.1 million Netflix shares in January 2022 and sold them in April after a subscriber miss, booking a loss above $400 million; its founder wrote that he had lost confidence in his ability to predict the company. The shares then rose roughly fivefold before the split. I would like Pershing Square, or anyone with its temperament and more patience, back on the register. The argument is not complicated. Netflix spends about 1.1 times its amortisation on content and does not need to spend more; it needs to say so, cap the budget, and return the rest. It raised prices in the United States, Mexico and Spain this year and the members stayed. It has $22.3 billion of buyback authority and a share price it can retire at about 20 times this year's earnings. The content arms race ended on October 6. Somebody should tell the capital budget.

Uber (UBER), which I also own, is the same trade in a different costume. Both went from growth at any price to disciplined cash machines with an advertising layer bolted on. Both generate $10 to $12 billion of free cash a year. Both sit at 52-week lows because the market, having spent a decade demanding they grow up, has decided grown-up companies are boring.
Netflix was paid $2.8 billion to lose. The market has charged it $200 billion for winning.

title: The bleach that stayed in the bottle
description: Clorox peaked at $240 in August 2020 and trades at $87 today. The safe trade is safe for a quarter and then it is a stock like any other.
body: Clorox (CLX) closed at $239.87 on August 5, 2020, the week it reported the fastest sales growth in its history, with every canister of disinfecting wipes in America sold before it reached the shelf. It closed at $87.36 on October 28, touched $79.12 on October 1, and sits 64 percent below a record six years old, worth about $10.5 billion. The product did not change. Bleach is sodium hypochlorite in water, and it did the same thing to a kitchen counter in 2019 as it does today. What changed was the fear, and fear was the only thing the 2020 price measured.

The thesis people still carry about this stock is that household products are the place to hide. The version I keep hearing cites a bank study showing home-goods companies beat the S&P 500 in volatile periods. I could not find the study and do not need it; the public record says the same thing more precisely. In 2022 the S&P 500 returned minus 18.5 percent and consumer staples lost less than one percent. In February this year, with technology selling off, staples led the index by 13 points. Clorox carries a beta of 0.57. When the market falls, this stock falls less. That part is true.

Here is the part the pitch omits. The staples trade is a put option with an expensive premium, paid in every year without a crash. Over the twelve months to October 2025 the sector returned minus 0.7 percent against 15.5 for the index. Clorox is down 27 percent in a year when the market rose. Its 52-week high, $128.90, came in February, during the volatility; by October the volatility had passed and so had the bid.

And the company has had a bad run at being boring. In August 2023 a cyberattack took down its order systems, slowed its factories and cut a quarter's sales by about $356 million, roughly a fifth. In 2025 it moved its American business onto a new ERP system, the kind of migration that is supposed to be invisible; retailers stocked up ahead of the switch and then ran inventories down, which Clorox says cost fiscal 2026 7.5 points of sales and 90 cents of earnings. Net sales fell 5 percent to $6.72 billion, earnings fell 26 percent to $4.81 a share. In April it closed the $2.25 billion purchase of GOJO, the maker of Purell, mostly with debt, taking borrowings to about $5 billion. A company that peaked on pandemic hygiene has just paid two billion dollars for more of it.

The dividend is the one thing that has behaved. Clorox has raised it for 48 consecutive years, most recently by a cent to $1.25 a quarter; at $87 the yield is 5.7 percent and the payout is 103 percent of trailing earnings. That ratio comes down if the ERP comparison washes out and GOJO adds the 9.5 points of sales promised for fiscal 2027; it does not if the chief executive's own word for the operating environment, "challenging," is the honest one.

So what is this stock? A phase-change artifact. In 2020 fear pushed the market across a boundary where the only thing anyone wanted to hold was the thing that kills germs, and Clorox was priced as if that state were permanent. Such states are not. The system relaxed, the premium evaporated, and what remained was a slow-growing bleach company at 18 times trailing earnings with debt it did not have before.

I do not own it. I would not short it; a 5.7 percent yield and a 0.57 beta will beat the index in the next crash, and there will be one. But the safe trade is safe for the quarter when nobody wants anything else. For the other nineteen quarters it is a stock like any other, with worse growth.
Safety is a price you pay every day for a day you cannot schedule.

title: The chokehold is in the chemistry
description: China mines 60 percent of magnet rare earths and separates 91 percent. The leverage was never in the ground. It is in the solvent.
body: A kilogram of dysprosium oxide costs about $200 in China this month and somewhere between $2,500 and $5,500 outside it. Terbium oxide is $900 inside and $10,000 to $13,000 out. Same molecule, same purity, a factor of ten to twenty for crossing a border. That spread is the price of a Chinese export licence, and the licence regime that produces it has now been in force for eighteen months, through three summits and two suspensions, with no sign of being lifted.

The dates matter because people keep conflating them. On April 4, 2025, Beijing put seven heavy rare earths, dysprosium and terbium among them, under case-by-case licensing. On October 9 it went much further: five more elements, controls on separation equipment, and an extraterritorial rule that would have required a Chinese licence for any magnet made anywhere containing 0.1 percent by value of Chinese material. When Trump and Xi met in Busan on October 30, China suspended the October package for a year, and Washington suspended its own Entity List affiliates rule, cut the fentanyl tariff and paused port fees. The April controls were never part of the deal. They are still there. Yttrium exports to the United States fell from over 333 tonnes in the eight months before the restrictions to 17 in the eight months after. Magnet exports to America ran at 512 tonnes in August, down 13 percent on the year; Chinese customs showed shipments to the US falling another 29 percent in September. General licences introduced last December cover three Chinese producers and exclude any defence end-user. Beijing confirmed on September 28 that the broader truce runs to January 10, 2027, and its statement did not mention rare earths by name. The suspension that was supposed to lapse on November 10 is, as I write, formally unextended.

So the chokehold is real. The question is where it sits, and most people have the geology wrong. China mines about 60 percent of magnet rare earths. That is a large share, but Mountain Pass in California is one of the richest deposits on earth, Lynas (LYC) mines in Western Australia, and Brazil, Vietnam and Greenland have ore. Rare earths are not rare. What China has is 91 percent of separation and 94 percent of sintered magnet production, and separation is the step that matters, because the fifteen lanthanides are chemically near-identical: same outer electron configuration, ionic radii that differ by a few picometres down the row. You cannot smelt them apart. You pull them apart with thousands of stages of solvent extraction, each stage exploiting a partition coefficient barely above one, and China spent thirty years and a great deal of poisoned groundwater learning how to run those cascades at scale. The leverage is a process. Processes are harder to copy than mines and easier to defend than tariffs.

Washington worked this out and did something I did not expect from this administration: it bought the process. In July 2025 the Pentagon put $400 million into MP Materials (MP) preferred stock and became its largest shareholder, guaranteed a floor of $110 a kilogram for NdPr for ten years, lent $150 million for heavy separation at Mountain Pass, and agreed to buy every magnet from a second Texas plant, 10X, that broke ground in February and should take US capacity to about 10,000 tonnes a year on commissioning in 2028. Apple signed for $500 million of recycled magnets from the Fort Worth plant the following week. MP's second quarter showed $17.6 million of price-floor income on NdPr realised in the high nineties; the first heavy-separation circuit reached mechanical completion in May. If I were going to own this trade I would own MP and Lynas, which this year is the only producer of separated dysprosium and terbium of any size outside China, at eight tonnes a quarter.

Eight tonnes. The world uses something like 180,000 to 200,000 tonnes of rare earth magnets a year and the United States imported about 40,000 of them in 2024, more than 90 percent from China. Vacuumschmelze is shipping from South Carolina, Noveon from Texas, and the IEA puts the bill for a diversified supply chain at around $60 billion over a decade, which is less than Meta borrowed in two years. The money is not the constraint. The constraint is that a solvent-extraction cascade takes years to commission and a decade to run well, and no fact sheet can shorten that.
The truce expires on a date in January. The partition coefficients do not expire at all.

title: The doll was a surveillance device
description: Germany banned a talking doll under its spy-equipment law. Alexa won the kitchen with no intelligence. Owning the room beats being smart.
body: In February 2017 the German Federal Network Agency, which regulates telecoms, ordered a blonde doll called My Friend Cayla off the shelves, on the grounds that an object which conceals a microphone and transmits what it hears is a prohibited surveillance device. Genesis Toys sold the doll, Nuance handled the speech, and the Bluetooth link had no authentication, so anyone within range could pair with a child's toy and listen. The regulator was not making a metaphor. It applied the law written for hidden bugs to a product in the toy aisle, and the law fit.

A year later the Federal Trade Commission settled with VTech for $650,000 over a tablet system that collected the names, birthdates and genders of hundreds of thousands of children without parental consent, was breached in 2015, and had told parents the data was encrypted when none of it was. Last September the FTC charged Apitor, a Shenzhen maker of robot toys, with letting a Chinese analytics kit called JPush pull precise location from thousands of children through its app; the $500,000 penalty was suspended because the company said it could not pay. Then came the chatbot plush. The Kumma bear from FoloToy, sold as running on GPT-4o, told testers how to find and light matches before moving on to sexual topics; OpenAI cut the developer off in November, and by February the bear was still offering GPT-5.1. Mattel announced its OpenAI partnership in June 2025, said its first product would arrive by year-end, then said not that holiday season. The toys are sensors pointed at the youngest people in the house, and the business model requires it.

Which brings me to the sensor that won. Amazon put the Echo on sale on November 6, 2014, at $199, or $99 for Prime members with an invitation. It had seven microphones and almost no mind: music, weather, alarms, pitched fairly as a whole-home Siri. The Wall Street Journal later put the devices division's losses from 2017 through 2021 above $25 billion. Amazon could sell the hardware at a loss because the product was a microphone in the kitchen with a Prime account attached, and it has since shipped more than 600 million Alexa devices. Run the opposite counterfactual: a device arriving in 2025 with a frontier model inside. Smarter. It would have lost. The intelligence was always retrofittable; the countertop was not. Alexa+ reached everyone in the United States on February 4 this year, free with Prime, and 97 percent of the devices Amazon ever shipped can run it. A dumb device that owns the room upgrades into a smart one. A smart device that arrives late has to find a room.

Think of it as a phase transition. A room with a listening device in it is a different state of matter from a room without one, and the energy barrier is the first installation. Once the microphone is there, making it cleverer costs a software push; making a cleverer microphone appear in that kitchen costs a second purchase nobody makes.

That is why the ethics of the toy aisle are not a side issue. Mattel and its imitators are not competing on intelligence; the intelligence is rented from the same handful of labs. They are competing to be the first microphone a child trusts, and the retention policies tell you what the prize is. The amended children's privacy rule took full effect on April 22; a bill to update the underlying law passed the Senate unanimously in March and is stalled in the House. The German regulator understood in 2017 what the American market still prices as a feature: a device that hears a child is a device that hears a child, whatever its face is.
Cayla has been illegal in Germany for nine years. The room she was built to occupy was taken by a speaker.

title: The elevator is the only tenant that never leaves
description: Otis sells the elevator at a 5 percent margin and services it at 25 for decades. The annuity hiding inside every building is the business.
body: There are about 23 million elevators and escalators in service on earth, and the count grows at a mid-single-digit pace because every new building needs one and almost no old building gives one back. Otis (OTIS) maintains about 2.5 million of them, roughly one in nine. That is the largest service book in the industry and a smaller share than the company's fame suggests; I have heard "a fifth of the world's elevators" from people who should know better. It moves 2.5 billion people a day with 72,000 employees, 45,000 of them in the field with a toolbag.

The share is not the number that matters. The split is. Last year Otis sold $5 billion of new equipment and earned $240 million on it, a margin under 5 percent. It sold $9.4 billion of service, maintenance, repair and modernization, and earned $2.37 billion, a record 25.1 percent margin. Service was 65 percent of sales and 91 percent of segment profit. The new elevator is the razor, sold near cost to get into the shaft. The service contract is the blade, sold every month for as long as the building stands, and a building changes owners, tenants and names far more often than it changes elevator contractors.

In my own field this is the difference between nucleation and growth. Forming the first droplet of a new phase costs free energy; the barrier is high and most attempts dissolve. Once a droplet exists above its critical size, growth is downhill and nearly free. Installation is the nucleation event, and Otis pays for it at a 5 percent margin. Everything after is growth.

The trouble is that nucleation has slowed where it used to happen most. Global new-equipment units fell 6 percent last year to 735,000, driven by a 13 percent drop in China, and Otis's own Chinese new-equipment sales and orders both fell by high-teens percentages last quarter. China is about a fifth of its new-equipment sales and 11 percent of total sales. In July the company cut its 2026 earnings guidance to $4.01 to $4.05 a share from $4.20 to $4.24. The stock is down 18 percent in twelve months to about $75, 19 times earnings, a 2.3 percent dividend, a $28.6 billion company. Deutsche Bank has it as a short-term sell, Wells Fargo started it at underweight, and the chief executive retires next summer.

Here is what the sellers have right. A Chinese apartment boom that is not coming back means fewer razors installed in China for years, and every unit not installed in 2026 is a service contract not signed in 2028 and not renewed in 2040. The damage is real, and it is slow, which is the worst kind for a stock because it never produces the single bad quarter that clears the air.

Here is what they have wrong. They are pricing a company that earns 91 percent of its profit from service on its 9 percent new-equipment problem. The maintenance portfolio grew 4 percent for the fourth consecutive year. Modernization, the business of ripping out a 1990s controller and keeping the shaft, grew 24 percent last quarter with a backlog up 24 percent, because an installed base ages whether or not anyone is building. The 23 million units already installed are the market. The 735,000 new ones a year are the marketing.

Otis was spun out of United Technologies on April 3, 2020, three weeks into a pandemic, and has spent six years explaining to a market that wanted a machinery stock that it is a subscription business with a factory attached. I would rather own the blades than the razor, and at 19 times earnings I would rather own them a little cheaper than this. But nobody has ever moved into a building and asked who made the elevator. Everybody knows who they call when it stops.

title: The metal that named the trade
description: Up to nine million American homes still drink through lead pipe banned in 1986. The rule to remove it runs to 2037, and the pipe is patient.
body: Lead is soft enough to bend around a corner by hand, which is why the Romans ran it under their cities and why the people who did the running were called plumbers: plumbum gave the trade its name. The United States banned new lead water pipe in 1986. By the Environmental Protection Agency's count, up to nine million homes are still connected to the main through the old stuff, and in October 2024 the agency finally wrote the rule that makes water systems dig it out: all of it, within ten years of a compliance date that lands in late 2027. The last lead service line is scheduled to leave the ground around 2037. A line laid the year before the ban will be fifty-one years old by then.

The chemistry is why this took a century. Lead does not leak into water on its own schedule. A pipe carrying properly treated water grows a passivation film on its inner wall, a thin scale of insoluble lead carbonate and phosphate between the metal and your glass, and as long as nobody touches the water chemistry the film holds. Change the source, drop the orthophosphate, let the pH drift, and the film dissolves and the metal comes with it. That is what Flint was: a passivation layer, removed. The new rule lowers the action level from 15 to 10 micrograms per litre, but a limit is a measurement, not a fix. The fix is the trench.

The economics are not close. The agency puts the cost of the rule at $1.5 to $2 billion a year and the benefits at $13 to $25 billion: up to 900,000 infants a year spared low birth weight, 1,500 fewer premature heart deaths, 200,000 IQ points not lost. Thirteen dollars back for one in. No private balance sheet is allowed to make that trade, because the dollar comes out of a water bill in 2029 and the thirteen come back as a child who reads a little better in 2045. So the pipe sat there through the 1991 rule and the 2021 rule and is only now being counted.

Here is what I find strange about water, more than roads or wires. It is the one utility where the asset is older than the institution. Roughly 67,000 water systems fall under the rule, most of them small, and the lead under their streets predates the system's charter, its ratepayers, its engineers and often the municipality itself. A power line is replaced on a depreciation schedule. A lead service line was never on one, because nobody expected to replace it; the plan was to coat it and hope.

Who pays for the trench. Washington put up $15 billion from the 2021 infrastructure law for lead lines specifically and $26 billion usable for lead at all, against an annual bill the agency itself puts near $2 billion for a decade, so the balance lands on the water bill in the towns least able to pay it. The water utilities' own trade association sued over the rule the month it was published, on the grounds that ten years is not feasible; the government has defended it through two administrations, briefing closed in April, and the court hears argument this autumn. Meanwhile the rule stands: inventories and first replacements are due November 1, 2027, and the agency issued fresh guidance in August on how to reach the pipes. It sells the programme as 15,500 jobs per billion dollars, which is true and the wrong reason. The country has about 510,000 plumbers and pipefitters for nine million trenches.

If I wanted to own the shovel rather than the hole, I would look at Pentair (PNR), which sells the pumps and filters that sit between a dubious main and a kitchen tap, and Advanced Drainage Systems (WMS), which extrudes pipe from recycled plastic for the water that falls on the street rather than the water that comes out of it. Neither has a lead problem. Both get paid when somebody decides to fix one.
The metal named the trade. So far it has outlasted every rule written about it.

title: The panel was never the hard part
description: A module leaves China for under ten cents a watt and still waits years for a wire. The cheap part of solar is the only part that got cheap.
body: In May 2025 China connected 93 gigawatts of solar to its grid in a single month. The modules had fallen below ten cents a watt at the factory gate the year before, a price that buys the tempered glass, the aluminium frame, the encapsulant, the junction box and the sliced silicon that turns photons into current, and the factories were losing money at it: prices down more than 60 percent since 2023, margins at the largest producers around minus ten percent, close to $5 billion of cumulative losses since the start of 2024. The cheapest electricity-generating object ever built is sold below cost by an industry that cannot stop.

Every stage upstream is Chinese too: about 92 percent of the world's polysilicon, 98 percent of its wafers, more than 90 percent of its cells, four fifths of its modules, and China is the main maker of the glass and the encapsulant film besides. The IEA expects concentration in the key segments to stay above 90 percent through 2030. First Solar (FSLR) is the one real exception, and it got there by leaving silicon out: a cadmium telluride film a few microns thick deposited straight onto glass in Ohio, the one large module maker a tariff on Chinese silicon cannot touch.

So the panel is solved. Why is solar still hard here? Because the panel is the only part that got cheap, and the rest is priced in American hours and American permits. A rooftop job is a crew, an inverter, racking, an electrician, a permit, a utility inspection and a salesman, and the panel is now a minor line on that invoice. GAF Energy's solar shingles and Tesla's solar roof are both attacks on the labour side of the same problem: if the roofer is already up there, let the roof be the panel. Utility scale is worse. The IEA's own words for the United States are grid queue backlogs and interconnection delays, and a project in a queue pays interest on land it cannot energise.

A megawatt is a rate and a megawatt-hour is an amount: a 100-megawatt farm makes 100 megawatt-hours in a bright hour and nothing at midnight, and the grid is paid for the second number while being built for the first.

In a chain of reactions the overall rate is set by the slowest step, and speeding up the fast ones changes nothing. China spent a decade making the panel step effectively instantaneous. The slow step in America is a transformer order, a county permit and a utility engineer with a queue, and Washington has lately made it slower. The residential tax credit died at the end of 2025. Utility-scale projects must be in service by the end of 2027 unless construction began within a year of the new law. Foreign-entity rules now reach into the Chinese supply chain, which is the only supply chain, and Chinese cells and modules carry a 50 percent Section 301 tariff besides. The IEA cut its forecast for American solar by almost 40 percent, 140 gigawatts less by 2030, and for residential by almost 70. Constellation (CEG), the country's largest nuclear operator, is the opposite bet and the same bet: firm power from plants already connected, and the connection is the asset.

People keep telling me solar quadruples by 2030. It does not. The IEA's main case has the world's renewable capacity a little more than doubling, 4,600 gigawatts added between 2025 and 2030 with solar nearly 80 percent of it, and solar's share of the world's electricity going from 8 percent to 15. Call it a doubling, carried by a country with a desert and a grid it orders rather than queues for: China is nearly 60 percent of the growth and will have solar above a fifth of its own generation by 2030.
The sun is free everywhere. The paperwork is priced locally.

title: The sticker does the work
description: A television does not change when it goes back through the return door. Its price does. Most of investing is noticing that gap.
body: A 65-inch television costs what the shelf tag says it costs until the moment someone carries it back through the door. Then it costs something else. Nothing happened to the panel. The pixels did not age in the eleven days it sat in my living room. But the store cannot put it back on the shelf as new, so a second sticker goes on the box, and the second sticker says open box, and open box means a discount, and the discount is often large.

So here is a small game I play. Buy the television. Return it inside the window, intact, receipt in hand. Come back a few days later and find the same unit on the clearance rack wearing the second sticker. Buy it again. Pay cash on at least one leg, preferably both, because I would rather the loyalty database not draw a line between the two transactions, and because a game the store would prefer you did not play is still a game you are allowed to play.

I am not writing this to teach anyone how to shave a few hundred dollars off a Hisense. I am writing it because it is the cleanest demonstration I know of a fact most people never fully absorb: price is not a property of the object. Price is a story the seller tells about the object, and the story can be rewritten by events that never touch the thing itself.

Physicists have a name for a quantity that depends only on the state of a system and not on its history. The television is a state function. Its price is not. Its price carries a path: who held it, for how long, whether a box was opened, whether a form was filled in. The retailer's accounting cannot see the panel. It can only see the path.

Markets do this at scale, every day, with better instruments. A bond gets cut one notch below investment grade and every fund whose mandate forbids junk must sell it that week, whether or not a single cash flow changed. A stock falls out of an index and the index funds dump it on rebalance day. A company reports one bad quarter and the word distressed goes on the box. Same cash flows, new sticker. Someone who is only permitted to own clean boxes has to sell to someone who is willing to look inside.

That second buyer is who I try to be. Not because open boxes are always bargains; they are not, and sometimes the panel really is cracked. But the discount for a damaged label is paid by people who are not allowed to check and collected by people who are.
The return desk is the most honest counter in the store. It is where the seller admits, in writing, that the first price was only ever a story.

title: Three envelopes
description: Three firms own three quarters of chip-design software. Washington took the pencil by letter in May 2025 and handed it back in forty days.
body: On Friday, May 23, 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security sent Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) a letter. Siemens EDA got one the same day, and the following Thursday Synopsys (SNPS) received its copy and suspended its guidance the same day. A licence was now required to export, re-export or transfer within China any electronic design automation software, including software classed so low on the control list that it normally needed no licence at all. The day the news leaked, Cadence fell 10.7 percent and Synopsys 9.6. Three envelopes, and most of the world's chip design was under licence.

Three was enough because three is the industry. Synopsys has about 31 percent of global EDA revenue, Cadence about 30, Siemens about 13: three quarters of the market and roughly 80 percent of China's. Siemens' Calibre, which checks a layout against a foundry's rules before tape-out, is used by nine in ten chip designers on earth. A chip is a drawing before it is a thing, and the drawing is made in software owned by two Californian companies and a division of a German conglomerate.

I write Rust, so I see this as the difference between a check at compile time and a check at runtime. Chip controls are runtime checks: a rule names a part number, customs inspects each shipment, smugglers test the coverage one crate at a time. Controlling the design tools is a compile-time check. Nothing unpermitted gets built, because it never gets drawn. That is what the letters did, and why the industry went quiet: nobody was told what remained permissible, so the three companies stopped almost everything.

In practice there was a hole. Software already installed on a Chinese desk kept running; what stopped was updates, patches and support. The compiler stayed, frozen at its last version, and a frozen compiler designs yesterday's chip forever. That bites hardest at the frontier, where every new node needs new tool releases, and barely at all on the mature nodes where China ships its volume. A licence on software is a slow strangulation, not a cut.

It lasted forty days. On July 2 Synopsys received a second letter: the restrictions were rescinded, effective immediately. Cadence and Siemens followed a day later. The price was rare earths. Under the framework agreed with Beijing, China would speed its permits for magnets and critical minerals, and America would let chip-design software, ethane and aircraft engines flow again. The most complete chokepoint in American technology was spent on a truce over dysprosium. China's hold on rare earths is a chemical process that takes a decade to copy. America's is software, and last summer the two were put on one table and swapped.

The money explains some of it. Synopsys took about $990 million from China in fiscal 2024, 16 percent of revenue; Cadence $550 million, 12 percent. Empyrean, the largest Chinese vendor, took about 1.2 billion yuan that year, roughly $170 million, and has sat on the Entity List since December 2024; Primarius and a hundred-odd smaller firms share the rest. Synopsys's China sales alone are nearly six times Empyrean's whole business, and every month under the letters sent Chinese purchase orders to Empyrean instead, which is how a chokepoint builds its own replacement. Synopsys, meanwhile, closed its $35 billion purchase of Ansys in July 2025 and now sells the physics as well as the logic: heat, stress and electromagnetics under the same roof as timing. The pencil got heavier. This year's fight has moved downstream, to lithography tools and who may service them in China.

My bet would be the three, not the chips. A chip gets sanctioned by name, one part number at a time. The software it was drawn in has no part number and, at the frontier, no substitute, and the one time Washington picked it up, it put it down after forty days.

title: Three hundred thousand dollars a bed
description: Two companies hold most of ICE detention. Washington now buys their buildings, pays them to run them, and cannot FOIA either one.
body: On July 2 the Department of Homeland Security paid CoreCivic (CXW) $1.5 billion for two detention centers in California, and on August 4 another $734 million for two more in Kansas and Minnesota: 7,187 beds for $2.2 billion, which the company's own release works out to $307,000 a bed. On October 5 GEO Group (GEO) sold its Adelanto complex in the Mojave, 2,644 beds, for $950 million, or $359,000 a bed. ICE's median daily rate for a bed is $92. In every case the seller stays on to run the building; GEO's contract runs to 2029 with an option to 2034. The government bought the asset and kept the operator.

The line that two companies own half of America's private prisons is roughly true and misses the point. Private prisons hold about 8 percent of state and federal prisoners, and GEO and CoreCivic are most of that trade, but prisons are not where the money is. Immigration is. About a third of ICE detainees sit in GEO facilities and roughly a quarter of ICE's beds are CoreCivic's; 86 percent of detainees were in for-profit hands when this administration took office. ICE was 48 percent of GEO's $2.63 billion of revenue last year and about 42 percent of CoreCivic's in the first quarter of this one. Between them the two booked about $4.8 billion in 2025.

What changed is one number. On January 20, 2025 ICE held 39,314 people. By July 30 this year the average daily population was 67,180, after a January peak above 73,000, and the count of authorized facilities had doubled from 134 to 272. The law signed on July 4, 2025 put $45 billion into detention through September 2029, against an annual detention appropriation that had been about $3.8 billion. GEO took its ICE capacity from about 20,000 beds to 26,000 in a year, the most new business in its history. CoreCivic now guides to $1.5 billion of net income in 2026, because selling four buildings to your largest customer books as a $1.8 billion gain. Both raised their buybacks within days of closing, GEO to $1.25 billion, CoreCivic to $1.2 billion with $500 million of it executed at once.

The other complaint is that these companies owe the government nothing. It is backwards. They are contractors, and in this contract the obligations run toward them. ICE agreements carry guaranteed minimums, beds paid for nightly whether anyone sleeps in them, and an analysis of ICE's own July data found about 8,200 such beds standing empty at more than $1.2 million a day. The GAO's September report is titled, in full, Immigration Detention: Urgent Planning Needed to Avoid Further Waste of Taxpayer Dollars. What flows the other way is harder to see. The Freedom of Information Act does not reach a private operator, and a bill to change that has been introduced since 2005 and never passed. ICE's detention standards are not written into law. The acting director of ICE since June spent about a decade as a GEO executive. Thirty-nine people died in ICE custody in the twelve months to January, the most in any year since the agency was created in 2003, twenty-seven of them in privately run facilities.

I would not own either stock, and the reason is structural before it is moral. Every business I own has a growth metric I can reason about: subscribers, payment volume, syrup. The growth metric here is the number of human beings the executive branch decides to confine, which went from 39,000 to 73,000 in a year and which the next administration, appropriations fight or court order can move the other way with a signature. GEO has traded between $12.51 and $33.17 over the past twelve months and closed at $27.57 on October 28, at thirteen times earnings. That is the chart of a referendum.
The government owns the buildings now. The companies are still paid by the bed.

title: Three neutrons, ten years
description: The AI companies are buying power from reactors that already exist. New uranium demand lands in the 2030s; only the term price has noticed.
body: Earlier this month, in Covert Township, Michigan, workers lowered fuel assemblies back into a reactor that was shut in 2022 and sold to be dismantled. The Energy Secretary toured Palisades this week and said it will be running within weeks, on up to $1.52 billion of federal loan guarantees. In Pennsylvania, Constellation (CEG) expects fuel on site by year-end for the 835-megawatt unit it has renamed Crane and everyone else still calls Three Mile Island, under a twenty-year contract to sell the output to Microsoft. No shuttered American reactor has ever come back. Two are, one of them for a software company.

Count the gigawatts the AI companies have signed for, then count the new ones. Meta's 6.6 gigawatts by 2035, announced in January, is more than 2.1 from Vistra (VST) plants that have run for decades, 1.2 from an Oklo campus pencilled for 2030 at the earliest, and TerraPower reactors due no sooner than 2032. Amazon's 1,920 megawatts from Talen's (TLN) Susquehanna comes out of a plant already on the grid. Every deal has the same shape: output from reactors that already hold fuel. A change of customer is not a change of demand.

Which explains the strangest chart in commodities. The long-term contract price, the one utilities actually pay, ended September at $96.50 a pound, a nominal record above the $95 of 2007. Spot sat near $90. Uranium equities are down over 20 percent in a year, and the Sprott trust that does nothing but hold the metal traded this month at an 11.6 percent discount to what it holds. The term price is set by people buying fuel for 2030; the equities by people who wanted the trade to pay in 2026 and have left. I side with the fuel buyers.

Supply sits in one place. Kazakhstan produced 25,839 tonnes of uranium in 2025, about 40 percent of the world, nearly all of it by pumping sulphuric acid into sandstone, 70 to 80 kilograms of acid per kilogram of metal. Kazatomprom (KAP) has cut its nominal 2026 capacity about 10 percent, and Rosatom's Uranium One owns half or more of several of its mines. Mines covered about 90 percent of reactor requirements in 2024; the rest came out of stockpiles, and stockpiles do not refill.

But the mine is not the chokepoint. The chokepoint is three neutrons. Natural uranium is about 0.7 percent U-235, a reactor wants 3 to 5, and the only route is to turn the metal into uranium hexafluoride gas and spin it. Fluorine has a single stable isotope, so the whole difference between a molecule carrying U-235 and one carrying U-238 is three neutrons in roughly 350 mass units, and a centrifuge exploits it a sliver at a time, in cascades thousands of machines long.

Rosatom owns about 29 million of the world's 68 million separative work units, 43 percent. American utilities bought 26 percent of their enrichment from Russia in 2025, under a 2024 law that bans the trade and whose waivers expire on January 1, 2028. Urenco adds 700,000 units in New Mexico by early 2027. Centrus (LEU), with a $900 million federal contract signed in July, expects no new commercial capacity before 2029.

Lay the dates in a row. Power contracts signed in 2024 through 2026. Restarts fuelled in 2026 and 2027. Russian waivers lapse at the start of 2028. Western centrifuge halls arrive from 2029. The first reactors that are new rather than renamed arrive between 2030 and 2035, and a thousand-megawatt unit then wants about 140,000 separative work units a year for life. None of that is priced into a share of Cameco (CCJ) trading on this quarter's spot. My bet would be Cameco and Centrus, held through the stretch where nothing appears to happen.
The fuel going into Palisades this month already exists. The fuel that matters does not, and neither do the centrifuges that will spin it.
